title: Bill Ward (musician) - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 100,419. William Thomas Ward, born 5 May 1948, Aston, Birmingham. Played drums as a child to 1940s big bands; early influences Gene Krupa, Buddy Rich and Louie Bellson, later Larrie Londin, Bernard Purdie, Joe Morello, John Bonham, Ringo Starr and John Densmore. Sang and drummed in the Rest; Mythology with Tony Iommi; then Earth with Ozzy Osbourne and Geezer Butler, renamed Black Sabbath. On the albums from Black Sabbath (1970) to Never Say Die! (1978), and on Heaven and Hell (1980) and Born Again (1983); left the Heaven and Hell tour in 1980 and again after Born Again, replaced by Bev Bevan; reunions at Live Aid (1985), 1992, 1994, 1997-1999 and Ozzfest 2005; left the 2012 reunion over a contract, replaced by Brad Wilk on 13. Sang It's Alright (Technical Ecstasy) and Swinging the Chain (Never Say Die!). Early equipment Ludwig and Slingerland, Zyn and Zildjian cymbals, Speedking pedals; now Tama and Sabian. Rolling Stone's 100 greatest drummers (2016), no. 42. Butler on Rat Salad: 'Bill used to fill out a whole 45 minutes doing a drum solo just to get rid of that 45 minutes.' Heart attacks in 1998 and 2017; played at Back to the Beginning, Villa Park, 5 July 2025.

title: Jeff Potter, 'Bill Ward: Metal Drumming Godfather', Modern Drummer, June 2020 (posted 1 May 2020)
notes: 'I heard a lot of big band music. I was drawn to drummers, and particularly to Krupa.' Krupa 'reckless', 'almost sloppy' yet in control; Buddy 'always seemed tight and professional'; Krupa's kick patterns heard in Earl Palmer's on Little Richard's records; the intro of Wicked World 'I stole that from Krupa'; New Orleans funeral music from about six. 'I play orchestration; I play back to what comes at me.' 'I build structures around things.' 'I never thought about keeping a beat in Black Sabbath.' 'It has to be behind': an on-top feel 'would have completely ruined everything'. Half time 'or just a really simple right-hand pattern' to make a song feel slower. 'Dynamics were everything.' Into the Void: 'hold everything on the ground', watching Iommi's left foot, no fills, 'the song is about the band, not me'. Mitch Mitchell and John Densmore 'orchestrational' drummers, Mitchell's playing 'totally like' his own approach. 'The only thing I really needed to hear was the very top of Tony's high notes'; 'I had to play really hard'. A 1965 memory of John Bonham and the bass drum. Early 1970s kit: Ludwig in Black Oyster, 3-ply, 9x13 tom, 16x18 floor tom, 14x22 bass drum, 5x14 chrome 400 snare; Super Zyn cymbals, 14-inch hats, 16- and 18-inch crashes, a 20- or 22-inch ride. Today: Gretsch Brooklyn in Gray Oyster, two 18x24 bass drums, a 26-inch china 'on rare occasion'.

title: Mark Griffith, '2024 Modern Drummer Hall of Fame: Bill Ward', Modern Drummer, 1 December 2024
notes: Only the introduction read (the interview is for subscribers). 'His drumming has a unique swing, a patience, and a reckless abandon that no one else's drumming has.' 'He created a style of drumming that can be imitated but will never be duplicated.'

title: 'Bill Ward Talks About Influences, Black Sabbath's Early Days', Blabbermouth.net, 27 October 2005 (from an All About Jazz interview)
notes: Excerpts of an All About Jazz interview. Before five or six 'all the music that I ever heard was jazz and it was American jazz, and it was big-band jazz'; 'I am probably attracted to it because of the drummers that played in those big swing bands'. The songs 'came out of big jams'. 'We were very hungry young men when we wrote Black Sabbath and when we wrote War Pigs.'

title: Tim Coffman, 'Iron Man: the Black Sabbath song Bill Ward called a disappointment', Far Out, 5 April 2024
notes: Quotes Ward from Planet Rock (no date): 'I had some disappointments, especially with the bass drum sound on Iron Man'. The author hears 'Ward galloping away on the tom-toms at the outro'.

title: Black Sabbath (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 109,943. Evil Woman and Wicked World at Trident on 10 November 1969; the rest at Regent Sound, Denmark Street, on 17 November 1969 in one twelve-hour session, played live with almost no overdubs. Released 13 February 1970 (Vertigo). Producer Rodger Bain. Ward: 'I think the first album is just absolutely incredible'; on the song Black Sabbath, 'I was playing drums to the words'. N.I.B.'s title from Ward's beard.

title: Paranoid (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 132,440. Recorded 16-18 June 1970 at Regent Sound and Island Studios, London; released 18 September 1970 (Vertigo). Producer Rodger Bain. Ward drums on all but Planet Caravan, congas on it. The title song an afterthought: 'We didn't have enough songs for the album, and Tony Iommi just played the guitar lick and that was it' (Ward). War Pigs grew from a jam in Warning. Rat Salad Ward's drum solo. Joe Levy on Ward and Butler's 'Visigoth rhythm section'.

title: Master of Reality - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded at Island Studios, London, 7-15 February and 6-13 April 1971; released 6 August 1971 (Vertigo). Producer Rodger Bain. Ward drums, percussion on Children of the Grave. Ward (2016): 'I went for bigger bass drums, also experimenting with overdubs.' Into the Void the hardest track for him.

title: Vol. 4 (Black Sabbath album) - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded May-June 1972 at the Record Plant, Los Angeles; released 22 September 1972. Produced by Black Sabbath and Patrick Meehan (Iommi in practice). Mojo: 'the seismic Supernaut (a favourite of Frank Zappa, featuring Bill Ward's soul-inspired breakdown)'. John Bonham counted Supernaut among his favourite songs.

title: Sabotage (Black Sabbath album) - Wikipedia
notes: Recorded February-March 1975 at Morgan Studios, Willesden, London; released 28 July 1975 (US). Produced by Black Sabbath and Mike Butcher. Symptom of the Universe cited as one of the earliest examples of thrash metal; its last section an improvisation in the studio. Ward 'especially favouring the backwards cymbal effect'.
